summary: Wrath, honor, and grief among warriors: Achilles' rage at Agamemnon, his revenge on Hector for Patroclus, and Priam's plea, inside a coalition war fought for Helen.

hunger.why: Feasts and sacrificial meals punctuate the camp; Achilles refuses food in grief, then shares a meal with Priam, but food is never a struggle.

thirst.why: Wine libations and the rivers Scamander and Simois appear, yet no character seeks or lacks water.

feeling-cold-hot.why: Hephaestus' fire boils the river Scamander and the Trojans try to burn the ships, but temperature extremes are brief episodes.

sleepiness.why: Zeus sends Agamemnon a deceptive dream, Achilles cannot sleep for grief, and the night raid of Odysseus and Diomedes exploits sleeping Thracians.

curiosity.why: Diomedes and Odysseus scout the enemy camp by night, but exploration of new places is marginal in a siege fixed around one plain.

explanation-seeking.why: Calchas explains the plague's cause and seers read omens, but mysteries are quickly answered by gods and prophets.

skill-acquisition.why: Phoenix recalls raising Achilles to be a speaker and doer; warriors test their prowess in aristeia, yet little training is shown.

play.why: The funeral games for Patroclus fill a whole book with chariot racing, boxing, wrestling, and footraces.

resource-accumulation.why: Prizes of honor drive the plot: Briseis and Chryseis as spoils, stripped armor, ransoms, and Agamemnon's offered gifts.

resource-foraging.why: Raids on neighboring towns are recalled, but searching for scarce resources is not part of the action.

mental-time-travel.why: Zeus's plan, Nestor's strategies, Achilles' choice between two fates, and foreknowledge of Troy's fall and Achilles' death shape every decision.

fear-of-predators.why: Lions, boars, and wolves appear only in similes; no character faces a predatory creature, though dogs and birds threaten the dead.

fear-of-aggressors.why: The whole poem is open battle: spears, chariots, sieges of the ships, and duels with Hector, Diomedes, Ajax, and Achilles.

fear-of-heights.why: Hephaestus recalls being hurled from Olympus and fighters contest the Trojan walls, but heights carry little dread.

disgust.why: Apollo's plague rots the camp, flies threaten Patroclus' corpse, and Hector's body is dragged to be defiled by dogs.

pain-aversion.why: Hundreds of wounds and deaths are described anatomically: spears through temples, bowels spilled, Hector's heel pierced.

pride.why: Kleos, undying glory, is the warriors' goal; each hero's aristeia, boasts over fallen foes, and prizes of honor mark success.

shame.why: Aidos governs the fighters: Hector refuses to retreat for shame before the Trojans, Paris is shamed into dueling, Agamemnon admits his folly.

moral-pride.why: Hector stays to defend Troy knowing it will fall, and Achilles keeps his oath of withdrawal at great cost.

guilt.why: Achilles blames himself for sending Patroclus to die, and Agamemnon acknowledges his blindness and makes amends.

warmth.why: Patroclus is remembered for gentleness, Hector tenderly reassures Andromache, and Achilles comforts the grieving Priam.

moral-blame.why: Achilles denounces Agamemnon's greed, Hector and Helen rebuke Paris, Thersites attacks the kings, and gods censure the dishonoring of Hector's corpse.

moral-praise.why: Hector is mourned as Troy's bulwark, Patroclus praised for kindness, and Achilles honored for returning the body.

revenge.why: Achilles' vengeance for Patroclus drives the second half; Menelaus seeks Helen back from Paris; Hector's killing of Patroclus answers Sarpedon's death.

forgiveness.why: Achilles accepts Agamemnon's gifts and reconciles, then yields Hector's body to Priam, ending his rage in shared mourning.

compassion.why: Patroclus weeps for the dying Greeks, gods pity Hector and the Trojan women, and Achilles pities Priam's helpless grief.

affiliation.why: Glaucus and Diomedes seal guest-friendship and exchange armor, and the embassy to Achilles tries to win him back as an ally.

friendship.why: The bond between Achilles and Patroclus, and its loss, is the emotional core of the poem.

sadness.why: Grief saturates the poem: Achilles' mourning for Patroclus, the laments of Andromache, Hecuba, and Helen, and Priam's weeping.

humor.why: Thersites' railing, the gods' squabbles, Aphrodite wounded and whining, and Hera seducing Zeus provide comic relief.

embarrassment.why: Paris slinks away from Menelaus and is scolded, Thersites is beaten before the army, and Agamemnon is exposed by his false test of the troops.

reasoning.why: Assemblies and councils dominate: the quarrel in Book 1, the embassy's speeches to Achilles, Nestor's advice, and divine debates on Olympus.

coalitional-affiliation.why: The Achaean confederation against Troy and its allies, plus the gods split into two camps, structure every event.

status-seeking.why: The plot begins with a rank dispute: Agamemnon asserts kingship by seizing Briseis, Achilles demands due honor, and heroes rank themselves by prizes.

envy.why: Agamemnon resents Achilles' greater prowess, Hera and Athena resent Aphrodite's prize, and Zeus's favor is contested, though longing for others' goods is secondary.

anger.why: The poem's first word is wrath: Achilles' rage at Agamemnon, then at Hector, and the fury of Agamemnon, Zeus, and Hera.

hatred.why: Achilles wishes to eat Hector raw, drags his corpse, and sacrifices Trojan captives; Hera's loathing of Troy is unrelenting.

romantic-affiliation.why: Paris and Helen's attraction, Hector and Andromache's tenderness, and Hera's seduction of Zeus are present but subordinate to war.

sexual-attraction.why: Helen's beauty makes elders excuse the war, Paris draws Helen to bed, and Hera arouses Zeus with Aphrodite's belt.

long-term-love.why: Hector and Andromache's marriage, Achilles' claim to love Briseis as a wife, and Odysseus' longing for Penelope show enduring bonds.

desire.why: Paris drags Helen to bed after the duel, and Zeus lists his many conquests before lying with Hera.

romantic-jealousy.why: Menelaus fights Paris to recover Helen, Agamemnon takes Briseis to spite Achilles, and Hera resents Zeus's lovers.

sexual-jealousy.why: The war itself stems from Paris taking Menelaus' wife, and Achilles rages that Agamemnon will sleep with his captive.

sexual-disgust.why: Helen loathes Paris after his cowardice, and Phoenix recalls his mother urging him to lie with his father's concubine.

kin-sexual-disgust.why: No incest appears; the marriage of Zeus and Hera as siblings is treated as normal.

parental-care.why: Hector lifts Astyanax and prays for him, Thetis protects Achilles, and Priam risks his life to recover his son's body.

parental-investment.why: Thetis obtains divine armor for Achilles, Phoenix recounts raising him, and Peleus' parting advice is recalled.

familial-love.why: Priam's love for Hector, Thetis' for Achilles, Hector's for Paris and his household, and Hecuba's grief bind the poem.
